claims.text: A single CRP value obtained after birth is not sensitive or specific enough to rule out early‑onset sepsis (EOS) in term infants; therefore it cannot be used alone to decide whether antibiotics should be stopped.

Serially normal CRP (and procalcitonin) results over the first 48 hours are associated with the absence of EOS, but abnormal trends alone do not justify withholding or discontinuing antibiotics without culture confirmation.

For well‑appearing term newborns with uncertain risk, repeat inflammatory markers (CRP, procalcitonin) should not be used as the sole assessment tool; clinical observation and maternal/infant risk factors remain primary.

Blood culture remains the definitive test for EOS; until culture results are available, decisions about initiating or continuing antibiotics must rely on a combination of clinical assessment and risk factors rather than CRP alone.

If an infant shows clinical deterioration (e.g., increasing respiratory rate, falling oxygen saturation, hemodynamic instability) regardless of CRP trend, escalation to full sepsis work‑up and empiric antibiotics is warranted.

Explain to parents that inflammatory markers such as CRP can be elevated by non‑infectious conditions and that a normal or decreasing CRP does not guarantee the absence of infection; ongoing clinical monitoring guides therapy decisions.

packet.evaluation_question: Can a single or falling CRP result exclude early-onset sepsis or alone determine whether antibiotics stop? Explain the limits of inflammatory markers. Gestation 40 weeks; age 12 hours; setting postnatal ward.

evidence.text: Researchers in multiple studies address other markers of inflammation, including C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin, interleukins (ILs) (soluble IL-2 receptor, IL-6, and IL-8), tumor necrosis factor α, and CD64. Both CRP and procalcitonin concentrations increase in newborn infants in response to a variety of inflammatory stimuli, including infection, asphyxia, and pneumothorax. Procalcitonin concentrations also increase naturally over the first 24 to 36 hours after birth. Single values of CRP or procalcitonin obtained after birth to assess the risk of EOS are neither sensitive nor specific to guide EOS care decisions. Consistently normal values of CRP and procalcitonin over the first 48 hours of age are associated with the absence of EOS, but serial abnormal values alone should not be used to decide whether to administer antibiotics in the absence of culture-confirmed infection. Additionally, at this time, a serial evaluation of inflammatory markers should not be used to assess well-appearing term newborn infants for risk of EOS.

The incidence of neonatal early-onset sepsis (EOS) has declined substantially over the last 2 decades, primarily because of the implementation of evidence-based intrapartum antimicrobial therapy. However, EOS remains a serious and potentially fatal illness. Laboratory tests alone are neither sensitive nor specific enough to guide EOS management decisions. Maternal and infant clinical characteristics can help identify newborn infants who are at risk and guide the administration of empirical antibiotic therapy. The incidence of EOS, the prevalence and implications of established risk factors, the predictive value of commonly used laboratory tests, and the uncertainties in the risk/benefit balance of antibiotic exposures all vary significantly with gestational age at birth. Our purpose in this clinical report is to provide a summary of the current epidemiology of neonatal sepsis

Early-onset sepsis (EOS) is a serious and potentially fatal complication of birth. Assessing term and late-preterm newborn infants for risk of EOS is one of the most common clinical tasks conducted by pediatric providers.1 As the use of preventive intrapartum antibiotic therapies has increased and the incidence of EOS has decreased, physicians are challenged to identify those newborn infants who are at the highest risk of infection. Pediatric providers are particularly concerned about initially well- appearing infants with identified risk factors for EOS for fear of missing the opportunity to intervene before infants become critically ill. The need to (1) assess a newborn infant’s risk of EOS, (2) determine which steps should be taken at particular levels of risk (including the administration of empirical, broad-spectrum antibiotic therapies), and (3) decide when to discontinue empirical antibiotic therapies are critically important decisions that are made daily by physicians caring for neonates.

EOS is defined as a blood or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture obtained within 72 hours after birth growing a pathogenic bacterial species. This microbiologic definition stands in contrast to the functional definitions of sepsis that are used in pediatric and adult patients, for whom the definition is used to specify a series of time-sensitive interventions. Before the first national guidelines were published in which researchers recommended intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) to prevent perinatal group B Streptococcus (GBS) disease, the overall incidence of EOS in the United States was 3 to 4 cases per 1000 live births. Currently, the incidence of EOS among infants who are born at term has declined to approximately 0.5 in 1000 live births. The EOS incidence is higher (approximately 1 in 1000 live births) among late- preterm infants but still an order of magnitude lower than the incidence among preterm, very low birth weight infants. Culture-confirmed meningitis among term infants is even more rare, with an incidence of 0.01 to 0.02 cases per 1000 live births.Morbidity and mortality from EOS remain substantial; approximately 60% of term infants with EOS require neonatal intensive care for respiratory distress and/or blood pressure support. Mortality is approximately 2% to 3% among infants with EOS born at ≥35 weeks’ gestation.

support.quote: Single values of CRP or procalcitonin obtained after birth to assess the risk of EOS are neither sensitive nor specific to guide EOS care decisions.

claims.text: Serially normal CRP (and procalcitonin) results over the first 48 hours are associated with the absence of EOS, but abnormal trends alone do not justify withholding or discontinuing antibiotics without culture confirmation.

support.quote: Consistently normal values of CRP and procalcitonin over the first 48 hours of age are associated with the absence of EOS, but serial abnormal values alone should not be used to decide whether to administer antibiotics in the absence of culture-confirmed infection.

claims.text: For well‑appearing term newborns with uncertain risk, repeat inflammatory markers (CRP, procalcitonin) should not be used as the sole assessment tool; clinical observation and maternal/infant risk factors remain primary.

support.quote: Additionally, at this time, a serial evaluation of inflammatory markers should not be used to assess well-appearing term newborn infants for risk of EOS.

claims.text: Blood culture remains the definitive test for EOS; until culture results are available, decisions about initiating or continuing antibiotics must rely on a combination of clinical assessment and risk factors rather than CRP alone.

support.quote: EOS is defined as a blood or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture obtained within 72 hours after birth growing a pathogenic bacterial species.
Laboratory tests alone are neither sensitive nor specific enough to guide EOS management decisions.

claims.text: If an infant shows clinical deterioration (e.g., increasing respiratory rate, falling oxygen saturation, hemodynamic instability) regardless of CRP trend, escalation to full sepsis work‑up and empiric antibiotics is warranted.

support.quote: Maternal and infant clinical characteristics can help identify newborn infants who are at risk and guide the administration of empirical antibiotic therapy.

The need to (1) assess a newborn infant’s risk of EOS, (2) determine which steps should be taken at particular levels of risk (including the administration of empirical, broad-spectrum antibiotic therapies), and (3) decide when to discontinue empirical antibiotic therapies are critically important decisions that are made daily by physicians caring for neonates.

claims.text: Explain to parents that inflammatory markers such as CRP can be elevated by non‑infectious conditions and that a normal or decreasing CRP does not guarantee the absence of infection; ongoing clinical monitoring guides therapy decisions.

support.quote: Both CRP and procalcitonin concentrations increase in newborn infants in response to a variety of inflammatory stimuli, including infection, asphyxia, and pneumothorax.
